item.title: Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems
item.dc:creator: Giada Finocchio
Seraina Oberli
George D. Lampe
Michael Schmitz
Samuel H. Sternberg
Martin Jinek
item.description:
Authors: Giada Finocchio, Seraina Oberli, George D. Lampe, Michael Schmitz, Samuel H. Sternberg, Martin Jinek
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex 1,2 . Understanding the detailed mechanisms of this elaborate process is paramount to engineering CAST systems into programmable genetic tools 3–6 . Type I-F Pseudoalteromonas CAST ( Pse CAST) shows the highest activity in mammalian cells so far 7 and has been adapted extensively through directed evolution 8 . However, its continued rational engineering requires addressing critical gaps in our understanding of transpososome assembly and activation 9 . Here we perform structural analyses using cryogenic electron microscopy, validated by DNA transposition assays, to visualize the Pse CAST system in a series of functional states that define the stepwise mechanism of RNA-guided DNA integration. The structures of the Pse CAST targeting and transposase recruitment complexes revealed that conformational changes in the Cascade–TniQ module, induced by R-loop formation, are associated with target-DNA stabilization and TnsC heptamerization. This, in turn, results in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase by conserved interactions with the carboxy-terminal tail of TnsB. Finally, the structure of the 1.2 MDa Pse CAST transpososome holocomplex revealed allosteric coupling of TnsC–TnsB and TnsB–target-DNA interactions to the conformational remodelling of the TnsB catalytic site, activating donor-DNA integration. Together, these findings establish a unified mechanistic blueprint for RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs and provide a structural framework to guide their engineering for genome-editing applications.

item.title: Transcription from megabase-scale heterochromatin generates neural barcodes
item.dc:creator: Alex Buckley
Carlo Vetralla
Brendan Rose
Jash Gada
Gabrielle Servito
Antonina Hafner
Sedona Murphy
Michael Mui
item.description:
Authors: Alex Buckley, Carlo Vetralla, Brendan Rose, Jash Gada, Gabrielle Servito, Antonina Hafner, Sedona Murphy, Michael Mui, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Heterochromatin typically represses genes 1,2 , yet some genes paradoxically require it for activation 3–7 . How can the same chromatin environment both silence and promote transcription? Here we address this question by interrogating the clustered protocadherin (Pcdh) locus, where subsets of genes are stochastically expressed while most remain silent 8 . In neurons, stochastic and combinatorial expression of Pcdh genes generates unique cell-surface barcodes required for self–non-self discrimination and neural circuit assembly 8 . By combining RNA labelling of Pcdh genes and neurodevelopmental cell types with single-molecule chromatin tracing and stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy, we find that a compact heterochromatin domain containing Pcdh genes forms as these genes become activated during development. Pcdh transcription occurs within the compact domain and reads through downstream genes, and distal enhancers must access the domain to engage target promoters. Genetic perturbations in mice suggest that opposing genome folding forces cooperate to establish Pcdh locus architecture and promote stochastic Pcdh expression. Specifically, while DNA loop extrusion allows enhancers to breach heterochromatin and find target promoters, heterochromatin-driven compartmentalization supports an expanded enhancer–promoter search space. These findings shed light on a process foundational to the development of vertebrate nervous systems and suggest a mechanism for how transcription can occur within seemingly silent chromatin environments.

item.title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
item.dc:creator: Jianmin Wang
Jonathan A. Knott
Grant M. Domke
Brady S. Hardiman
Brian F. Walters
Songlin Fei
item.description:
Authors: Jianmin Wang, Jonathan A. Knott, Grant M. Domke, Brady S. Hardiman, Brian F. Walters, Songlin Fei
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Climate change and disturbances are reshaping forest ecosystems worldwide 1–4 , yet their combined effects on species redistribution remain poorly understood. Here we analyse repeated measurements from 44,368 forest inventory plots spanning 1999–2025, with an average remeasurement interval of 10 years, to examine how climate and natural disturbances jointly influence the elevational redistribution of tree species across the western USA. We show that climate warming increased sapling abundance, whereas increasing drought frequency and recent natural disturbances (fire, insect outbreaks and disease) reduced tree abundance, particularly among adult trees. By contrast, legacy fire was associated with increased sapling abundance, with stronger positive responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms. These influences were distributed unevenly across species’ elevational ranges: upper portions of species’ ranges generally experienced stronger warming, greater increases in drought frequency and more disturbance activity than lower portions, creating elevational asymmetries in stress and recovery. These elevational asymmetries were associated with more pronounced downslope shifts in basal area centres, probably reflecting disturbance effects on larger trees. By contrast, stem abundance centres showed more divergent shifts, consistent with sapling responses to both climate change and disturbance. Our findings reveal contrasting demographic responses to climate change and natural disturbances that shape the elevational redistribution of different species, with potential consequences for forest composition, resilience and long-term stability.
